title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: hereditary vice conceded; missing third — natural propagation
pass_a_gloss: The opponent then lengthens the chain: that first sin which doomed all is common either by each one's own deed or by imputation; not by own deed—Adam alone actually sinned—so by imputation to all. Why drop the third limb so often rung against Pelagians: natural propagation? The first sin crossed into us not as a fleeting act but as lasting aversion from God and turn to creatures as last end in Adam—and it crossed not by an imputation standing outside us, but by real sharing and propagation.
pass_b_english: So you press further. Now, you say, I assume that first sin which sentenced all men to penalty is common to all, either by their own act, or by imputation: Not by their own act, because Adam alone actually sinned. Therefore by imputation, because namely it is imputed to all. Why did you omit the third member so greatly sung against the Pelagians—or by natural propagation? For it is established that the first sin passed into us (not as it was a transient action, but as it was aversion from God and conversion to creatures as to the ultimate end, remaining in Adam)—passed, I say, not by an imputation which is outside us, but by true communication and propagation.
source_text: Itaque longius proveheris. Jam, inquis, assumo, primum illud peccatum quod omnes homines addixit poenae commune est omnibus, vel actu proprio, vel imputatione: Non actu proprio, quia solus Adamus actu peccavit. Ergo imputatione, quia scilicet omnibus imputatur. Cur tertium membrum omisisti tantopere adversus Pelagianos decantatum, vel propagatione naturali? Constat enim primum peccatum in nos transiisse (non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit aversio a Deo & conversio ad creaturas ut ad finem ultimum, permanens in Adamo) transiisse inquam non imputatione quae extra nos est, sed vera communicatione & propagatione.
